transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-18
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~75 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Alex Chen (Redwood SE), Rina Gomez (Redwood CSM), Jordan Lee (Spectral AI Head of ML), Priya Singh (Spectral AI Infra), Tom Martinez (Spectral AI CTO)

[00:00] Maya (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll do a deep dive on GPU runtime profiling and try to surface concrete perf win areas for your infra. Alex will lead the technical sections. Quick intros?
[00:22] Jordan: Jordan here, head of ML at Spectral, we run a couple of Llama-2 variants and some in-house fine-tuned models, mostly on A100 on prem, kubernetes. Latency SLOs are tight, p50 < 60ms for short prompts, p95 can spike.
[00:38] Priya: Priya, infra. We're managing clusters with k8s, using local NFS for weights today, exploring NVMe and MIG setups, and wondering about KMS integration and private deployment constraints.
[00:55] Tom: Tom, quick note on timeline - we want a pilot in July if the perf looks good.
[01:05] Alex (SE): Great. I'll cover kernel selection, CUDA graphs, and compare TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM. We'll also look at KV cache and batching tradeoffs.

[03:10] Alex: First, kernel selection. Runtime chooses different kernels based on layer type, seq len, and batch shape. In practice we see 2-3 hotspots: matmul/flash-attn kernels, softmax/normalization, and KV cache memcpy paths. If the kernel dispatcher picks a suboptimal GEMM kernel for certain seq lengths you lose 10-30% perf.
[04:02] Jordan: Are those choices dynamic per batch or per model load?
[04:10] Alex: Both. Most runtimes pick during compilation or first few iterations - vLLM tends to do more JIT-like choices at runtime; TensorRT-LLM compiles ahead with heuristics. That means vLLM can adapt but has more variance early, TensorRT often better steady-state but requires a good compile profile.

[06:20] Priya: We saw jitter with vLLM on short prompt workloads, sometimes the first few tokens are slow. Is that warm-up?
[06:30] Alex: Yep, that's either kernel warm-up or inefficient graph paths before caching. CUDA graphs reduce per-launch overhead by pre-capturing the execution graph; for chat workloads with variable lengths you need graph reuse strategies - e.g., capture graphs for common prefix lengths, fall back for tails. But graphs don't magically fix kernel selection mismatches.

[09:10] Tom: How big is the win if we add CUDA graphs and optimized kernel selection? Ballpark numbers?
[09:20] Alex: For our internal benchmarks we saw 15-35% lower p95 latency when combining kernel tuned builds + CUDA graphs on A100 for medium-sized models (3B-13B), depending on sequence distribution. For very large models the memory tradeoffs and KV cache pressure matter more.

[11:00] Jordan: Can you elaborate on KV cache behavior - we rely on long context for agent memory, so KV size gets large and memory bandwidth looks like a bottleneck.
[11:12] Alex: Sure. Two things: memory layout and memcpy patterns. If KV cache is interleaved or causes non-coalesced loads it kills throughput. Redwood runtime attempts to use contiguous pinned buffers and prefetch/async copy patterns; we also do selective sharding of KV across GPUs for larger contexts. But that adds complexity with routing and recomposition latency.

[13:45] Jordan: So sharding KV would help throughputs but hurt single-request latency because of cross-GPU comms?
[13:53] Alex: Exactly. For latency-sensitive short-context calls you want non-sharded KV and local memory. For high-throughput long-context you shard and accept some cross-GPU NCCL overhead. We presented hybrid policies: low-latency tier keeps recent KV local; archival KV can be sharded or even spilled to NVMe with async fetch.

[17:30] Priya: About quantization - we tried 4-bit quant on some weights and saw mixed quality. Latency improved but p95 still variable. How aggressive do you go?
[17:45] Alex: Quantization gives big memory and throughput wins, especially int4/int8 on TensorRT-LLM. But quantization-aware calibration matters. We recommend per-layer calibration and sanity evals; for embeddings and softmax layers being FP16 often preserves quality. On some models we recommended mixed precision: int8 for matmul, fp16 for norms. That got 1.6-2x throughput on 8-bit-friendly kernels.

[21:05] Jordan: How does TensorRT-LLM compare to vLLM in your testing? We need reproducible steady perf in our on-prem clusters.
[21:15] Alex: Short version: TensorRT-LLM (TRT-LLM) trades more upfront compile time and tuning for predictable steady-state performance and excellent quantization support on NVIDIA HW. vLLM is flexible, faster to iterate, and sometimes better out-of-the-box for dynamic workloads because of its batching/eviction strategies. If you can afford compilation time and want best raw throughput/quantization, TRT-LLM is stronger. For quick dev cycles and variable workloads vLLM can be simpler.

[24:00] Tom: Any reliability concerns with TRT-LLM compiles on our cluster? We're air-gapped in parts.
[24:10] Alex: You can do offline compiles and ship tuned kernels. For air-gapped setups you'll need the private deployment package - Redwood Private supports offline kernel artifact distribution and KMS integration for keys. That avoids contacting external registries during compile.

[26:45] Jordan: Tell us about profiling - what's the recommended toolchain to capture relevant traces we should share?
[26:55] Alex: We typically use a combination: Nsight Systems for timeline and kernel-launch patterns, CUPTI for lower-level metrics, and custom counters in the runtime to log batch shapes, KV sizes, and kernel selection decisions. We also like to capture a traffic replay CSV with timestamps and tokens per call so we can synthetic-replay in a bench env.

[30:30] Priya: We'll be able to produce the replay logs. Is there a preferred format?
[30:35] Alex: CSV with columns: request_id, timestamp, model, prompt_len, completion_len, metadata - minimal. If you can include average tokens and distribution that helps, and sample model weights if allowed. We'll provide a secure S3 link.

[33:10] Jordan: Any tips for reducing p95 without hurting cost? We hate throwing more GPUs at it.
[33:18] Alex: A few levers: 1) Intelligent batching with latency budgets (small latency buckets), 2) Prefix caching - if many requests share common prompts, caching prefix KV gives big wins, 3) Quantized kernels for steady throughput, 4) CUDA graphs for kernel-launch overhead reduction. Also prefer priority routing (reserve capacity for low-latency traffic).

[36:50] Tom: We run k8s. How does Redwood integrate with our deployment model for Private?
[36:58] Rina (CSM): Redwood Private can be deployed as a customer-managed control plane; we support helm charts and an operator. For networking we'd recommend VPC peering and private endpoints; KMS integration for keys is supported. We'll share our deployment checklist.

[39:10] Priya: On the topic of kernel selection heuristics, do you do per-GPU microbenchmarks to pick best kernels per shape?
[39:20] Alex: Yes, we run microbenchmarks during the initial profiling phase. The runtime keeps a small perf table keyed by model layer shapes and seq/batch shapes; it uses that to pick kernels. It also supports manual overrides for customers who want to force a given kernel for compliance.

[42:30] Jordan: We worry about model updates causing perf regressions. What's your approach to detect and rollback?
[42:40] Alex: Redwood Optimize runs evals over prompt sets and tracks latency/regression alerts; we create canary rollouts and compare perf/quality. If a model or build regresses, automatic fallback to previous kernel set or model variant is possible while you investigate.

[45:00] Maya: Quick practical example - Alex, can you walk through a profiling artifact you'd share?
[45:06] Alex: Sure: 1) Nsight timeline with marked sections (tokenization, forward, KV copy), 2) CSV of per-request timing and batch shapes, 3) kernel selection log: mapping of layer shapes to kernel version and observed throughput, 4) a short replay harness to reproduce p95 with sampled traffic. We'll attach these to the perf spreadsheet.

[48:20] Priya: On CUDA graphs, how do you manage variable-length sequences?
[48:30] Alex: Strategy is to capture graphs for a matrix of common lengths and reuse when possible; for tails use a fallback path. Another approach is to pad to bucket lengths and run smaller graphs - padding introduces token waste but can still be net win for p95. We also maintain a graph cache with LRU eviction to limit memory.

[51:10] Jordan: Are there any gotchas with NVLink/NCCL when sharding KV?
[51:18] Alex: Yes: cross-GPU latency and collective op patterns can add jitter. For small batch sizes that's significant. Good practice: keep critical low-latency slices local, and schedule cross-GPU syncs asynchronously. Also monitor PCIe vs NVLink bandwidth and avoid unnecessary copies.

[54:00] Tom: If we run a pilot, what do you need from us to make the bench representative?
[54:07] Alex: Representative traces (csv), one or two model weights (or model spec), target SLOs and traffic mix, sample infra config (GPU type, memory, network). Also access constraints (air-gap, no external access) so we can prepare offline artifacts.

[57:30] Priya: Security - we need SOC2 and KMS integration details before any on-prem install.
[57:40] Maya: We'll send SOC2 summary and our Private deployment security whitepaper. KMS/HSM integration is supported; we'll include the KMS connectors doc.

[60:00] Jordan: Any comparisons you can share on latency vs cost for TRT-LLM quantized vs vLLM fp16?
[60:10] Alex: High-level: TRT-LLM int8 typically buys 1.5-2.5x throughput improvement and lower p95 vs vLLM fp16 given same GPU, but compile/tuning time and edge-case quality drops require evaluation. For cost we do per-token unit economics - we'll put concrete numbers in the spreadsheet after the replay.

[63:45] Maya: Let's recap next steps and owners. Alex will share perf artifacts, Maya will send pricing and security docs, Jordan will upload traces and models.

[64:00] Jordan: Yep, will do. We'll aim to upload by next Monday.

[71:20] Tom: Ok thanks everyone, excited to see results.

[71:28] Maya: Thanks, we'll follow up with calendar invites for kickoff and the S3 upload link.

[71:35] End meeting.

Notes: Transcript contains some automated transcription artifacts; some acronyms/misspellings possible (e.g., TRT-LLM, vLLM, Nsight sometimes transcribed as "n-side").
